rows.en: Not a small part of the explanations of the commandments and statutes that have become known and established among us date from the time of the Scribes. We have indeed seen that from the days of Ezra began the effort of the leaders of the generations to teach the people statutes and laws, so that they would keep and perform the commandments that had lapsed since ancient years. Now how many are the commandments in the Torah whose manner of performance is obscure and not explained in the Torah, and cannot be understood without the explanation that shows in what manner a given commandment is to be done! Therefore, if we say that in the days of the Scribes they practiced them, we must necessarily also say that the Scribes made known to them in what manner they were to be done, since we cannot imagine the performance of the act without the explanation. Now it cannot be denied that some of the explanations that teach us the manner of performing the obscure commandments were received traditions among them; this holds for the commandments that had not ceased since they were given: since they performed the act of the commandment, they necessarily also knew the necessary explanation. But for the commandments whose performance was not kept up among the people and was entirely forgotten, we must conclude that their explanation, which shows the manner of performance, was also forgotten, and they were compelled to explain them according to their own understanding in order to find the intent of the Torah. It is not for us to decide what was forgotten and what was kept, nor is it in our power to decide, because all the historical narratives whose source lies in these ancient days are silent and tell us nothing about the performance of the commandments. But in any case one thing is clear: the explanations of the kind we have mentioned are an inheritance to us from the Scribes, and it is all one to us whether they weighed and searched them out or whether they were received traditions in their hands. Explanations of this kind are: “And you shall take for yourselves on the first day” [Leviticus 23:40] — that the taking be by hand. “And the whole assembly of the congregation of Israel shall slaughter it at dusk” [Exodus 12:6] — that one slaughters for many. “Seven days you shall eat matzot” [Exodus 12:15] — that matzot are only from the kinds of grain. “The fruit of a goodly tree” [Leviticus 23:40] — this is the etrog. All these appear to be among the most ancient explanations. Close to this kind, among the remnants left to us from the generations of the Scribes, there are found in the books of the Oral Torah sayings whose character testifies that they are the work of the earliest sages, that is, the Scribes. The content of these sayings comprises necessary specifications for ordinances and laws that we have recognized as products of the Scribes; and since the specifications were necessary to them, it is self-evident that when the ordinances and laws were enacted, their specifications were made as well. The antiquity of these sayings is further recognizable by their brevity and simplicity. We have already said that the commandment of the recitation of the Shema is an ordinance of the Scribes; likewise the blessings before and after it are also very ancient in their root, and if we separate from them the many additions that were added to them, we recognize in them the work of the ancients, and they have rightly been ascribed to the generations of the Scribes (Zunz, p. 366). It is therefore self-evident that the Scribes already laid down the very rule that one must bless before and after it, and perhaps the very saying in which this rule is described in the Mishnah (Berakhot 1:4) is also theirs. So too is the matter with what is said concerning pe'ah, the first fruits and the appearance-offering [re'ayon] — that they have no fixed measure (Pe'ah 1:1); for this rule was already necessary to them from the time they took upon themselves to give the gifts of the priesthood and the Levites as written in the Torah. The sign of this saying's antiquity is its use of the word re'ayon, which we do not find again in the Mishnah; at a later time they used the word re'iyah in its place. Likewise the order of bringing the first fruits as described in the Mishnah (Bikkurim 3:2) contains very old sayings, without doubt from the time of the Scribes; and there is found the word paḥot [governors], which clearly points to the time when Israel was still under the rule of the Persians. Also the sayings of the Mishnah: “There are four principal categories of damages”; “Whatever I am obliged to guard, I have made ready its damage”; “property that belongs to members of the covenant” (Bava Kamma ch. 1) — from their language and their brevity it appears that they are very ancient and from the time of the generations of the Scribes (*Moreh Nevukhei ha-Zeman*, gate 13). It seems that the term bnei berit [members of the covenant] in this place does not refer to the members of the Israelite nation in that they bear the holy covenant in their flesh, but refers to them in that they entered together into the covenant in the days of Ezra and made a firm agreement to keep the Torah. There are further sayings in the Mishnah which we may suppose are from the time of the Scribes because their form resembles an explanation of Scripture: they include the words of the verse with the explanation attached to them, and this was precisely the way of the Scribes (Nega'im 12:5), as when it describes how the priest is to proceed in inspecting the afflicted house in order to declare it unclean. For all the sayings there, if we strip from them the additions (which were added at a later time, have a style like the style of the teaching⚠1 of the early Scribes (*Darkhei ha-Mishnah*, p. 5). Whoever investigates the matter will find further sayings of these kinds in the Mishnah and baraita that are to be ascribed to the Scribes. But we must be very cautious in our judgments, for it is not the brevity of a saying, nor even the style of its language, that alone testifies to its antiquity and to its coming from the time of the Scribes, unless we look at its content and subject. We must know that the most ancient explanations are also the simplest. For in the early time they did not yet go beyond the bounds of the plain sense of Scripture, they did not engage in the fine points of letters, and they did not yet know remote and strange midrashim. Also the fences and ordinances of the early time did not exceed measure as in a later time. Therefore the difference in character between the ancients and the later ones, in the midrash of the Torah, in fences and in ordinances, will be for us the line and plummet of judgment [Isaiah 28:17] when we judge the sayings set before us in the books of the Oral Torah, to know which of them is ancient and may be ascribed to the Scribes and which is a child of the later generations. For like a spring-fed stream that at its source is only like the palm of a man's hand [1 Kings 18:44], and little by little grows and swells until it becomes a rushing torrent, so it was with the exposition of the Torah. Its beginning was small [Job 8:7]. The plain sense of Scripture was the character of the midrash of the Torah. But in the course of time the studies were fruitful and multiplied, the explanations grew and the branches spread, because they derived one thing from another and the derivatives [toladot] multiplied.{v1_04_21:1} These derivatives had already ceased to have the character of explanations, for they did not in essence come out of the words of Scripture but came by way of logical reasoning, by likening one thing to another; and from their careful consideration of the laws of the Torah they arrived at specifications in the commandments and statutes. On the other hand, they had traditions in laws, statutes and judgments; in addition to this they weighed and searched out and enacted decrees, fences, ordinances and good customs. Now all these derivatives, specifications, traditions, fences and ordinances were a business for students and teachers to be occupied with [Ecclesiastes 1:13], and this was a great cause of change and difference in the way of study and in its spirit. For at first the men of understanding taught the people and the students the text of Scripture and explained to them its matter and intent; and to help the memory of the explanations, so that they would not be forgotten by the hearers — the people and the students — they needed no aid from outside, for whatever came out of Scripture directly, the text itself acted to remind the students of the explanation given to it. It was not so with derivatives and specifications that they derived by logical inference, or with matters founded on traditions, and all the more so with fences and ordinances, for none of which was there any hint in the Torah; therefore for all these they were compelled to clothe them in the garment of exact and short sayings, and to fix them as set rules, so as to make memory easier. A small remnant of such sayings from the Scribes is in our hands, and among them the testimony of Yose ben Yo'ezer (Eduyot 8:4), which comprises three sayings, and also other sayings mentioned above and many like them. The form of all of them and their brevity were fit to ease memory. Some of them are marked by numbers, for number acts strongly to fix the sayings recorded by it in the memory of the students. The sages of the Talmud spoke well on this (Yerushalmi Shekalim 5:1): that the Scribes made the Torah into counted items, for example: “Five may not give terumah.” Already Simeon the Just used this method in his saying, giving it a number when he said: “On three things the world stands.” And when they expounded the Torah more and more through reasoning and reflection, and derived various derivatives and specifications in the commandments and statutes, and when they went on to enact ordinances and to make fences for the Torah, so too sayings of this kind multiplied, comprising laws, statutes and specifications. These are marked especially by their brevity and the precision of their language, and they were given a special name by which they are called in the language of the sages: halakhah.

rows.en: The use of the word halakhah is very common in all the books of the Oral Torah. It is taken from Aramaic; its proper meaning is “law, custom,” and the Aramaean always says hilkheta where the Hebrew says mishpat in the sense of custom (*Musaf he-Arukh*).{v1_04_22:1} Hence every rule that comes from an act done among the people is called halakhah, as in “he saw an act and remembered the halakhah” (Sanhedrin 82a); and the rule that comes from the custom of the country is called hilkheta di-medinah (Kiddushin 38a). Halakhah is said of a matter agreed upon and received, in contrast to a matter that is argued by reasoning but on which there is not yet agreement, as in “If it is a halakhah, we will accept it; if it is a logical inference, there is a reply” (Yevamot 76b; Keritot 15b). Therefore the name halakhah came to be applied to every saying that comprises a fixed and agreed rule. And so they also used the word halakhah to indicate a decision in favor of one of two opposing views, and to fix the rule according to it, as in “and they fixed the halakhah permanently according to the words of the House of Shammai” (Yerushalmi Berakhot 1:1); and everything found in the Talmud as “the halakhah is according to so-and-so” is of this kind. By extension they used the word halakhah for fixed rules in matters that have no relation to the laws of the Torah; of this kind are “halakhot of proper conduct” (Berakhot 22b) and “halakhot of physicians” (Yerushalmi Yevamot 8:2); and likewise the rules of the combinations of the letters of the Name, by which — according to the belief of the sages of the Talmud — the world was created, they called by the name “halakhot of creation” (Sanhedrin 67b), and the rules of sorcery of all kinds they called “halakhot of sorcery” (also there). Under the concept of halakhah they also brought matters stated explicitly in the Torah, and called them “the bodies of halakhot” (Yerushalmi Shabbat 2:7), while the Babylonians called them “the bodies of Torah” (Shabbat 32a). In truth this name, “bodies of Torah,” is more common among the ancients (Ḥagigah end of ch. 1, and in the Tosefta there, ch. 2). And since they called the very words of the Torah by the name halakhah, we find that sometimes they also used the name halakhah for an explanation joined to Scripture, which we call midrash; for example: “through her a halakhah was newly established: an Ammonite man, but not an Ammonite woman” (Yerushalmi Yevamot 8:3). For this is nothing but a midrash that expounds the verse “An Ammonite or a Moabite shall not enter the assembly of the Lord” [Deuteronomy 23:4], which they explained as meaning just what is written: an Ammonite man, not an Ammonite woman. Some of the halakhot were described in short sayings, so that they were fluent in the mouth of all students, and they were called “regular halakhot” (Berakhot 22a). Similar to this is “the decided halakhah” (there, 31a), called “decided” because from the beginning of its foundation it was agreed and no one ever contested it; among the Jerusalemites (Yerushalmi there 5:1) it is called “the fixed halakhah.” The term halakhah is first found in the words of Hillel the Elder (Pesaḥim 66a, and in the Yerushalmi there); but it appears from his words that in his time the term “halakhah” was already commonly used to describe the concept now understood by it. Thus it follows from all this that every saying containing a fixed rule in the laws of the Torah — whether from what was received among them, or what is a derivative of the explanations, or a derivative of a derivative, or what was decreed and enacted to make a fence for the Torah; and likewise the decision of the sages in deciding between the views of their predecessors, or any decision in the court or in the house of study by majority, when they stood for a count and concluded the law decisively — every saying that comprises one of all these concepts is called by the name halakhah. During the generations of the Scribes the way of studying halakhah began; and from then on the halakhot were fruitful and multiplied and spread out exceedingly, and what at first was only a first trickle of water [Proverbs 17:14] became in the course of time a great and wide sea [Psalms 104:25], whose waters pass and flood over the Mishnah, the baraitot and the two Talmuds.
The antiquity of halakhah and its expansion.

One kind of halakhot is traced back to Moses at Sinai, and it too has a special name: “a halakhah [given] to Moses at Sinai.” Now since ancient times the expounders have differed from one another in their views about this kind of halakhah. The Jews who hold with perfect faith to everything handed down to them from their fathers also hold in their faith that this kind of halakhah is truly from Sinai, for so they received from their fathers. And since they received that the explanations and the fine points in the Torah, and all the halakhot in general, were handed to Moses at Sinai, they therefore believe that all the statutes, judgments and laws — except the decrees and ordinances — that were set down in the books of the Oral Torah we have today were all given to Moses at Sinai orally. Their faith grew so strong that a doubt never entered their hearts: perhaps their fathers, who received from their predecessors, and their predecessors from those who preceded them, up to the first generations — perhaps they erred in what they heard? Or perhaps the ancients did not mean to say so with exactness and precision? Nor did it seem strange to them, what they saw and knew: that from the days of Moses until after their return from the exile there is no speech and there are no words [Psalms 19:4] concerning the oral tradition, and the written Torah itself was abandoned and left in a corner; how then could an oral tradition, whose measure is longer than the earth [Job 11:9], have been preserved? All these doubts pass away before the strength of faith. Opposite these are the deniers. In ancient times these were the Sadducees, and after them the Karaites and all who walk in their footsteps; and they too did not try to investigate the matter: perhaps they would find matters that compel a tradition? Perhaps there are traces in the Torah itself of the existence of tradition, and perhaps they would find in the books of the Prophets and in the other Holy Writings matters that require its existence, or at least hints that would rouse and awaken their hearts to believe what many others believe? To all these doubts they paid no regard and gave no attention, but denied without investigation. There were indeed a few who expounded the Torah critically, whose hearts lifted them up to the inquiry, but they did not publish the results of their inquiry. Therefore this cornerstone, which is one of the most precious in the religion of the Jews, remained like an abandoned field, which diligent hands have not touched and over which the plough of criticism has not passed; and the little investigation that a few expounders offered it from time to time was no blessing but only brought up thorns over its face [Proverbs 24:31]. Now it will no longer seem strange to us if we see that belief, like denial, both grope for the wall like the blind [Isaiah 59:10]. Belief lacks its proper measure, and denial lacks the critical distinction between what is proven by demonstrations and what is vain and empty; therefore the one, having no right measure, believes everything, and the other, not distinguishing between good and bad, denies everything. But in order that we may know how to distinguish between the proven and the empty, and between the exact and the exaggerated, and in order to quiet the doubts that fall on this matter, we must get to the root of things. Against those who deny the very existence of tradition there is no need to reply, for we have already seen (above, ch. 1) that it is a clear matter, which cannot be denied even from the standpoint of criticism, that from the time the statutes of the Torah were written in a book they had traditions, without which several statutes in the Torah cannot be understood. We have also seen, from proofs that come from the Torah of Moses itself, that the necessity of explaining various statutes was there already from the beginning of the religion of the Torah and from the day it was founded. From all this it is surely proved (end of ch. 5) that what we have received from the ancients about the existence of matters of Torah handed down orally is not an empty thing. Therefore the existence of an oral tradition in general cannot be denied in any way, and whoever denies it is refuted by reason and by the truths set down in the history of our nation. But the doubt is very great with regard to the particulars. This doubt is: whether the explanations that are in our hands today and are included in the books of the Oral Torah were held in all the ancient generations with the same explanations by which it was explained from the beginning of its foundation, or were not held with certainty; rather, the ancients too, who received explanations from their predecessors, were in doubt whether they had received traditional matters or matters newly devised in some generation. And whether those halakhot that are designated by the name “halakhot from Sinai” were held so among them with certainty, or were not held with certainty but hung in doubt. We cannot resolve this doubt from what we know clearly and truly about the existence of explanations and traditional matters from the beginning of the religion of Moses; for the truth of the existence of some explanations and traditional matters is no conclusive proof that all the explanations and halakhot whose source we do not know were all founded from the start and from the earliest days of the religion of Moses. But in order to find the solution of the matter, we must return to the source and spread before us the words of the ancients themselves, so as to consider them and know their true view. For it is self-evident that we cannot attain what we seek except from their own words.

footnotes.en: They said of the decree on handling vessels on the Sabbath that according to the first decree (Tosefta Shabbat ch. 15) vessels may not be handled on the Sabbath except three: a knife for cutting pressed figs, a zomalistron [ladle] for a pot, and a small knife on the table. And they ascribed this (Shabbat 123b) to Nehemiah son of Hachaliah. Without doubt they relied on what they found in the book of Nehemiah 13, that he warned with great emphasis about the Sabbath; therefore they ascribed this decree to him as well. But if we consider the matter we easily find that it is not so. For this word zomalistron, which is a Greek name, already shows that this decree is late and cannot be earlier than the time of their acquaintance with the Greeks. For without doubt they did not know this utensil before the time of the Greeks, and it reached them only from them, together with its name; for had they known it, would it not have been called by a Hebrew or Aramaic name? Why did they name it with a Greek name? This being so, it follows that the decree too could not have existed before the time the Greeks came to the Land of Israel.

The measure of derivation has its foundation in Scripture, and the expounders derived one derivative from another. For example: the Torah said that whoever eats leaven shall be cut off [Exodus 12:15] — the derivative from this: “no leaven shall be seen with you” [Exodus 13:7]; and from this another derivative: “but on the first day you shall remove leaven” [Exodus 12:15]. These derivatives are written explicitly in the Torah. The derivative from “you shall remove” is: on the night of the fourteenth one searches for leaven; the derivative from this: a place into which leaven is not brought; the derivative from this: the law of the rows in the wine cellar. I have no proof that when the Scribes taught the verse “but on the first day you shall remove leaven” they had already derived all these derivatives; but it is hardly possible otherwise, for if the teacher instructs his student that it is a commandment to remove leaven from the house so that none will be found there on Passover, he will at once tell him to take care to search in all the places where one usually brings leaven, so that he will not find it on Passover. So one thing came out of another, whose first root was Scripture, and in its derivatives the root was no longer recognizable.

It seems to me that already in Scripture the root halakh is used in this sense, as in “She looks well to the ways [halikhot] of her household” (Proverbs 31), whose meaning is conduct. And the written form hilkhot would accordingly be the plural⚠1 of the noun halakhah in the construct state.
